rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2, 4.1 - authors built an IoT weather station and embedded prototype in tomato greenhouses in Tulancingo, Hidalgo, recorded data every 10 min for 365 days, trained MLP ANN models. Q2: Section 4.1-4.2, Fig. 9 (data versus ANN model, summer and winter), Fig. 10 and Table 6 - ANN prediction of inside greenhouse temperature compared with measured data, monthly R2 80-97%, annual adjusted R2 95.8%; Section 4.3, Tables 11-12, Figs. 12-13 - fuzzy associative memory maps predicted and cropland temperature to PWM activation of the anti-frost sprinkler pump in five frost classes. Q8: Section 5 - authors state the method's disadvantage for R2 above 95% is the need for large amounts of data (10-min records over a full year); Section 3.1.1 - ROC performance obtained for one data partition, classifier not perfect, different architecture may do better. Q9: Table 1 - standard error and 95% lower/upper confidence limits for ROC area under curve of each input variable; Table 8 - standard errors of every regression coefficient per month; Table 6 and Section 4.2 - standard deviation of residuals per monthly model.
rows.notes: The study validates the temperature prediction against real greenhouse measurements and presents the fuzzy controller design and output table, which matches the passage as literally worded. However, it never measures whether activating the anti-frost sprinkler actually kept the greenhouse microclimate warmer during a frost; the regulating effect itself is asserted from the ice-barrier concept, not observed. Q3: ROC analysis and ANOVA/regression are two statistical treatments of the same sensor dataset, not independent methods. Q4: no measurement of the insulation mechanism (ice sheet, heat loss) through which sprinkling would regulate temperature. Q5/Q6: one site, one crop (tomato greenhouses); monthly models are not sites. Q7: the data-volume requirement is stated as a disadvantage rather than a condition for the regulation effect; fuzzy/ANN suitability remarks are generic. Q9: doubt - the standard deviation of residuals is close to a validation error (RMSE-type), but Table 1 reports true 95% confidence limits and Table 8 coefficient standard errors, so counted as yes.

rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2, 4.1-4.3 - own IoT prototype, year-long 10-min weather data, ANN models and fuzzy controller developed and tested in tomato greenhouses in Hidalgo, Mexico.
rows.notes: The study contains no result on water use, water saving, irrigation scheduling efficiency or crop water requirements. Its ANN predicts greenhouse inside temperature and its fuzzy system triggers a sprinkler that wets the greenhouse plastic cover for frost protection; water volume applied is never quantified, and no comparison with any conventional irrigation practice is made. What the study shows is prediction accuracy of inside temperature (R2 80-97%) and a rule table for anti-frost pump activation. The ML-driven system is an anti-frost sprinkling controller rather than an irrigation-scheduling tool for crop water use, so it is a related but different application of the technology, and the claimed effect (water conservation) is simply not addressed.

notes: Full text appears complete (abstract through references). The paper is primarily a system-development and model-validation study: ANN temperature prediction is checked against measured greenhouse data, but the anti-frost sprinkler's effect on greenhouse temperature and any water-use outcome are not measured. Table 11 contains inconsistent inequality notation but does not affect the ratings.
